"'''Smithereens'''" is the second episode of the fifth series of the British science fiction [[anthology series]] ''[[Black Mirror]]''. Written by series creator and showrunner [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by [[James Hawes]], it premiered on Netflix on 5 June 2019, alongside "[[Striking Vipers]]" and "[[Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too]]". In the episode, the [[Ridesharing company|rideshare]] driver Chris ([[Andrew Scott (actor)|Andrew Scott]]) takes hostage the intern Jaden ([[Damson Idris]]) of Smithereen, a large social media company, making a demand to contact the company's [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] Billy Bauer ([[Topher Grace]]).

The episode was inspired by an experience Brooker had in a car hired via [[Uber]] when the driver got out unexpectedly to get a bottle of water. He also began a story around how a person grieves the loss of a loved one differently when their life is permanently inscribed in social media. Smithereen is similar to the social media website [[Twitter]] and Bauer was compared to its CEO at the time, [[Jack Dorsey]]. Most filming took place in England, but Grace's scenes were filmed in Spain. Scenes were shot roughly in chronological order, at Scott's request, and his inability to drive was a challenge for the production.

The major theme in "Smithereens" is the power social media companies wield and their products' adverse effects, primarily their designed addictiveness. Critical reception was mixed: Scott's acting received widespread praise and a nomination for a [[Primetime Emmy Award]], but reviewers mostly criticised the episode's storyline and the simplicity of its message. It was ranked poorly compared to other 'Black Mirror' installments.

==Plot==
Chris Gillhaney ([[Andrew Scott (actor)|Andrew Scott]]) is a [[ridesharing company|rideshare]] driver in London. He has sex with Hayley ([[Amanda Drew]]), a woman from his [[group therapy]], who has been trying to guess the password to her late daughter's Persona account to find out what led to her suicide. One day, Chris picks up Jaden ([[Damson Idris]]), an employee at the social media company Smithereen. Chris abducts him at gunpoint but is furious upon discovering that he is a newly joined intern. A police officer sees Jaden in the back seat with a bag over his head and pursues with her partner. In the chase, Chris veers to avoid two teenage cyclists and stalls the car in a field. An additional contingent of police arrive, led by [[Chief superintendent|CS]] Linda Grace ([[Monica Dolan]]).

Chris aims to speak with Smithereen [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] Billy Bauer ([[Topher Grace]]). He sends a picture of Jaden at gunpoint to Jaden's superior. Word gets to [[Chief operating officer|COO]] Penelope Wu ([[Ruibo Qian]]) in the U.S., who speaks to Chris. However, Billy is on a solitary retreat. As police visit Chris's listed address, Smithereen gather much more information through Chris's social media profiles. Formerly a teacher, Chris lost his fiancée Tamsin in a car accident with a drunk driver three years earlier and has been planning a kidnapping for weeks. The hostage negotiator David Gilkes ([[Daniel Ings]]) speaks to Chris, but Chris has researched negotiator tactics and leverages the hostage so that David leaves.

Smithereen record Chris while he is on hold. Chris notices the police's behaviour changes after he lies to Jaden that the gun is fake; bystanders overhear the police and post the misinformation on social media. He threatens to shoot Jaden in five minutes unless Billy calls him; despite Penelope and the FBI's protestations, Billy does so. Chris reveals that he believes himself responsible for the car accident that killed his fiancée; he was checking a Smithereen notification when the cars collided, but the other driver was blamed. Chris and Billy agree that Smithereen has been designed to be as addictive as possible and Billy says he was planning to quit as CEO. Chris implies he will now kill himself, but Billy begs Chris to let him help. Chris thinks of a last favour: ask Persona to give Hayley her daughter's password.

Chris tries to release Jaden, who urges Chris not to attempt suicide and then fights to take his gun off him. At Grace's orders, snipers fire into the car as the pair struggle. Around the world, people check their phones, then continue on with their lives.

==Production==
{{external media|video1="[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2SybklT8k1k Black Mirror: Smithereens]"<br />The trailer for "Smithereens".}}
A fifth series of ''Black Mirror'' was commissioned by Netflix in March 2018, three months after the release of series four.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-renewed-season-5-at-netflix-1090957|title='Black Mirror' Renewed for Season 5 at Netflix|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|last=Strause|first=Jackie|date=5 March 2018|access-date=9 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234537/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-renewed-season-5-at-netflix-1090957|url-status=live}}</ref> Initially part of series five's production, the [[interactive film|interactive]] work ''[[Black Mirror: Bandersnatch]]'' increased in scope to the point where it was separated from the series and released as a standalone film; it premiered on 28 December 2018. Although previous series of the programme produced under Netflix contained six episodes, series 5 comprises three episodes, as series creator [[Charlie Brooker]] viewed this as preferable to making viewers wait longer for the next series.<ref name="DS S5">{{cite news|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27568474/black-mirror-season-5-episodes/|title=Exclusive: Black Mirror's Charlie Brooker reveals why season 5 only has 3 episodes|website=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Jeffery|first=Morgan|date=23 May 2019|access-date=5 June 2019|archive-date=24 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524045833/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27568474/black-mirror-season-5-episodes/|url-status=live}}</ref> The three episodes—"[[Striking Vipers]]", "Smithereens" and "[[Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too]]"—were released on Netflix simultaneously on 5 June 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/tv/a27475929/black-mirror-smithereens-striking-vipers-season-5-trailer-release-date-photos-cast-spoilers/|title='Black Mirror' Season 5 Takes On Home Robots And Romance Apps In Dark New Trailer|work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|last=Ovenden|first=Olivia|date=15 May 2019|access-date=9 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234551/https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/tv/a27475929/black-mirror-smithereens-striking-vipers-season-5-trailer-release-date-photos-cast-spoilers/|url-status=live}}</ref> As ''Black Mirror'' is an [[anthology series]], each instalment can be watched in any order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://heavy.com/entertainment/2019/06/do-you-have-to-watch-black-mirror-episodes-in-order/|title=Do You Have to Watch 'Black Mirror' Episodes In Order?|work=[[Heavy (website)|Heavy]]|last=Dwilson|first=Stephanie Dube|date=4 June 2019|access-date=5 June 2021|archive-date=25 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225154915/https://heavy.com/entertainment/2019/06/do-you-have-to-watch-black-mirror-episodes-in-order/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Conception and writing===
"Smithereens" was written by Brooker, who wanted the series to contain an episode without any futuristic technology, to remind viewers that ''Black Mirror'' is not solely a science fiction show. Previous such instalments include the first episode, "[[The National Anthem (Black Mirror)|The National Anthem]]", and season three's "[[Shut Up and Dance (Black Mirror)|Shut Up and Dance]]".<ref name="ew"/> The two initial sparks for "Smithereens" were a question about how a person deals with the loss of a loved one whose life has been recorded in social media and an experience in a rideshare car booked through [[Uber]]. In the latter, the driver unexpectedly got out of the car and looked for something in the boot, while Brooker realised he was unaware of where they were. The driver was just getting some water.<ref name="Independent interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-interview-season-5-annabel-jones-smithereens-striking-vipers-a8936981.html|title=Charlie Brooker interview: 'The Black Mirror stories are not warnings. Technological progress is inevitable'|work=[[The Independent]]|last=Shepherd|first=Jack|date=5 June 2019|access-date=5 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234537/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-interview-season-5-annabel-jones-smithereens-striking-vipers-a8936981.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Smithereens - Persona.png|thumb|alt=Persona|The grieving Hayley aims to access her daughter's social media account on the fictional website Persona.]]
The former idea developed into a story where the protagonist was trying to get into the social media account of somebody who died by suicide, but Brooker thought it would be "extremely superficial and cheap, and also weirdly slightly intrusive" to give a "glib reason" for a character's suicide. In the final episode, the secondary character Hayley has this storyline, but the contents of her daughter's Persona account are not shown. Brooker said, "Really, she's probably just going to open another box of questions by going in there".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27677089/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-ending-explained-charlie-brooker/|title=Black Mirror season 5 'Smithereens' ending explained|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Jeffery|first=Morgan|date=5 June 2019|access-date=6 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234538/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27677089/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-ending-explained-charlie-brooker/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] described Chris as "overwhelmed" and said that he "feels like an onlooker" over society. Discussing the psychological effects of technology, Brooker said that he used to "reach for a cigarette first thing in the morning" as a chain smoker, and now does the same thing with his smartphone for a "similar reward-feedback loop".<ref name="Dazed">{{cite web|url=https://www.dazeddigital.com/film-tv/article/44794/1/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-annabel-jones-andrew-scott-smithereens-interview|title=Charlie Brooker: 'I just reach for my phone on autopilot'|work=[[Dazed]]|last=Gorton|first=Thomas|date=10 June 2019|access-date=5 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234538/https://www.dazeddigital.com/film-tv/article/44794/1/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-annabel-jones-andrew-scott-smithereens-interview|url-status=live}}</ref> Jones gave the example of a homescreen showing the number of unread emails as [[gamification]], one of many features that witness how phones are "subtly and incrementally{{nbsp}}... designed to absorb you".<ref name="Independent interview"/>

Billy Bauer was written to embody a [[Silicon Valley]] entrepreneur: Brooker said that Billy thinks himself a "switched on, liberal, hippy kind of guy".<ref name="Dazed"/><ref name="IGN interview"/> He was not written to be a "cartoon villain" or resemble any particular social media CEOs, though Brooker did take inspiration from a ten-day retreat taken by then-[[Twitter]] CEO [[Jack Dorsey]]. Jones commented that Billy is "as lost as" Chris and feels "out of control".<ref name="ew" />

Brooker described the episode's ending, in which strangers are seen looking at their phones, as a message about how the characters' lives were "reduced to ephemeral confetti that just passes us by".<ref name="ew">{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-smithereens-ending/|title=''Black Mirror'' creator explains that 'Smithereens' ending|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Hibberd|first=James|date=5 June 2019|access-date=5 June 2019|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605090450/https://ew.com/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-smithereens-ending/|url-status=live}}</ref> The "most important day" of Chris's life and maybe Jaden's is "reduced to the level of a pop-up".<ref name="IGN interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2019/06/07/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-ending-and-billy-bauer-explained|title=Black Mirror Season 5: 'Smithereens' Ending Explained by Charlie Brooker|work=[[IGN]]|last=Griffin|first=David|date=8 June 2019|access-date=5 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234538/https://www.ign.com/articles/2019/06/07/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-ending-and-billy-bauer-explained|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Casting and filming===
[[File:Topher Grace 2019 by Glenn Francis.jpg|thumb|alt=Topher Grace|[[Topher Grace]], a fan of the series, played Billy Bauer in the episode “Smithereens”.]]
Having previously talked to Brooker about appearing, Scott joined the cast of "Smithereens" as he was "really gripped by [the main] character."<ref name="ScottInterview">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2020/biz/news/hot-priest-andrew-scott-black-mirror-smithereens-1234652625/|title=After Hot Priest and Hamlet, Acclaimed Actor Andrew Scott Takes a Dark Turn in 'Black Mirror'|date=25 June 2020|first=Bob|last=Verini|website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115163317/https://variety.com/2020/biz/news/hot-priest-andrew-scott-black-mirror-smithereens-1234652625/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref> He described himself as less interested in technology than "the idea of the vulnerability of people that a simple mistake can be made at any given moment and you can blame it on yourself or you can blame it the powers that be".<ref name="Dazed"/> Per Scott's request, most of the episode was shot in chronological order, so that he could "slowly reveal" more of Chris's character. He said he was "as playful as possible" when acting, aiming to perform "in as many different ways as possible".<ref name="ScottInterview"/> One difficulty in filming was that Scott did not know how to drive a car. Production mounted a car on top of a mobile platform and instructed Scott to mimic steering to go along with filming.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27809564/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-andrew-scott-driving/ | title = Black Mirror's 'Smithereens' star Andrew Scott reveals how they got around him not being able to drive | first = Rianne | last = Houghton | date = 7 June 2019 | access-date = 7 June 2019 | website = [[Digital Spy]] | archive-date = 7 June 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190607143044/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27809564/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-andrew-scott-driving/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

Topher Grace—who had recently filmed for ''[[BlacKkKlansman]]'' (2018)—played Billy Bauer. He had been looking to vary the types of characters he played and was a fan of the show, having particularly enjoyed season two's "[[Be Right Back]]" and other episodes which "are more emotional than technology-based".<ref name="THR"/> He was surprised while reading the script when he reached Billy's appearance, having built up an expectation that he would be more villainous.<ref name="THR"/><ref name="Vulture interview"/> He said that similar tech company founders had "created their own legend" and that he expected Billy to stand out in a crowd and have a distinctive "relationship with spirituality". For this reason, Grace wanted Billy to be bald but after discussion he ended up with a [[Bun (hairstyle)|bun]]. Grace told an interviewer that he was unsure of whether Billy was "as trapped as he says", but that he does not personally like "people like this".<ref name="Vulture interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/topher-grace-black-mirror-interview.html|title=How Topher Grace Became a 'Digital God' for Black Mirror|date=5 June 2019|first=Kathryn|last=VanArendonk|website=[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200924025344/https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/topher-grace-black-mirror-interview.html|archive-date=24 September 2020|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref> Damson Idris played the Smithereen intern Jaden. His first ''Black Mirror'' audition was for the series three episode "[[Men Against Fire]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.looper.com/320762/damson-idris-star-of-outside-the-wire-exclusive-interview/|title=Damson Idris, Star Of Outside The Wire – Exclusive Interview|work=[[Looper.com|Looper]]|last=Lebovitz|first=David L.|date=27 January 2021|access-date=5 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234538/https://www.looper.com/320762/damson-idris-star-of-outside-the-wire-exclusive-interview/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Director [[James Hawes]] had previously directed "[[Hated in the Nation]]" in the third series.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/recap/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-smithereens/|title=''Black Mirror'' recap: 'Smithereens'|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Freeman|first=Luria|date=5 June 2019|access-date=5 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234553/https://ew.com/recap/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-smithereens/|url-status=live}}</ref> Most of the filming took place in England, overlapping with production of ''Bandersnatch''.<ref name="DS S5"/><ref name="ScottInterview"/> Urban scenes were filmed in various downtown London locations.<ref name="ScottInterview"/> Some footage was shot in [[Harrietsham]], [[Borough of Maidstone|Maidstone]] in Kent and in a field near [[Gravesend]] around June 2018. The Fairbourne Reservoir in Kent was used as a location for boardroom scenes.<ref>{{Cite news | url = https://www.kentlive.news/whats-on/whats-on-news/gravesend-maidstone-locations-feature-black-2944025 | title = The Gravesend and Maidstone locations which feature in Black Mirror's new episode Smithereens | first = Lauren | last = MacDougal | date = 7 June 2019 | access-date = 7 June 2019 | work = Kent Online | publisher = [[KM Group]] | archive-date = 7 June 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190607225814/https://www.kentlive.news/whats-on/whats-on-news/gravesend-maidstone-locations-feature-black-2944025 | url-status = live }}</ref> Grace flew to the UK to watch Scott's acting and briefly meet him before the filming of his scenes in Spain.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.goldderby.com/article/2020/topher-grace-black-mirror-smithereens-netflix-video-interview/|title=Topher Grace ('Black Mirror: Smithereens') on what geniuses have in common with each other [Exclusive Video Interview]|work=[[Gold Derby]]|last=Jacobsen|first=Kevin|date=18 June 2020|access-date=2 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234604/https://www.goldderby.com/article/2020/topher-grace-black-mirror-smithereens-netflix-video-interview/|url-status=live}}</ref> To help Grace match the emotional intensity of Scott during the phone call, an actor was hired to read Chris's lines offscreen—usually the person in such a role is not a professional actor.<ref name="THR">{{cite news | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-topher-grace-ending-his-episode-smithereens-1216318 | title = Why Topher Grace Doesn't Need to Tell You How His 'Black Mirror' Episode Ends | first = Jackie | last = Strauss | date = 7 June 2019 | access-date = 7 June 2019 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] | publisher = Valence Media | archive-date = 7 June 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190607225810/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-topher-grace-ending-his-episode-smithereens-1216318 | url-status = live }}</ref>

===Soundtrack===
The episode's music was composed by the Japanese artist [[Ryuichi Sakamoto]], known for his [[electronic music]] and soundtracks. It incorporates [[synthesisers]] which, according to ''[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]'' reviewer Daniel Martin-McCormick, create "rising tension", "a looming state of emergency" and are "steadfastly integrated" with the episode.<ref name="Pitchfork">{{cite web|url=https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/ryuichi-sakamoto-black-mirror-smithereens/|title=Ryuichi Sakamoto: ''Black Mirror: Smithereens''|last=Martin-McCormick|first=Daniel| website=[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]] |date=11 June 2019|access-date=6 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234604/https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/ryuichi-sakamoto-black-mirror-smithereens/|url-status=live}}</ref> The soundtrack was released as an album two days after the episode's premiere.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://music.apple.com/gb/album/black-mirror-smithereens-music-from-the-original-tv-series/1465902231|title=Black Mirror: Smithereens (Music from the Original TV Series)|last=Sakamoto|first=Ryuichi|author-link=Ryuichi Sakamoto|publisher=[[Apple Music]]|date=7 June 2019|access-date=6 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234604/https://music.apple.com/gb/album/black-mirror-smithereens-music-from-the-original-tv-series/1465902231|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Analysis==
[[File:Jack Dorsey 2014 (cropped).jpg|thumb|alt=Jack Dorsey|Many reviewers drew comparisons between Billy Bauer and then-[[Twitter]] CEO [[Jack Dorsey]].]]
Charles Bramesco of ''[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]'' and Matt Reynolds of ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' found the episode to have a [[police procedural]] style, similar to the third series episode "[[Hated in the Nation]]".<ref name="Vulture">{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-recap-smithereens.html|title=''Black Mirror'' Recap: Eyes on the Road|work=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]|last=Bramesco|first=Charles|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234604/https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-recap-smithereens.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Wired"/> Atypical for the genre, the gathering of intelligence is speedy, due to the power of the social media companies, rather than forming the majority of the episode's runtime.<ref name="Vulture"/> "Smithereens" is set in 2018; David Sims of ''[[The Atlantic]]'' said it "could've been pulled from today's headlines". He drew the connection that as with "The National Anthem", it showcases a news story which "begins to spiral out of control online".<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="Atlantic">{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review/590737/|title='Smithereens' Is the Only Flop of the New Black Mirror Season|work=[[The Atlantic]]|last=Sims|first=David|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605113540/https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review/590737/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'' reviewer Aja Romano found that it "blends a hefty mix of bleak nihilism and social satire" and "comes across like a thesis statement for the series as a whole".<ref name="Vox">{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/2019/6/5/18648965/black-mirror-smithereens-recap-season-5-review|title=Black Mirror's "Smithereens" wants to be the series' thesis statement. It falls utterly flat.|work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|last=Romano|first=Aja|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234605/https://www.vox.com/2019/6/5/18648965/black-mirror-smithereens-recap-season-5-review|url-status=live}}</ref> Louisa Mellor of ''[[Den of Geek]]'' saw a "[[black comedy]] of errors" in Chris's plan quickly going wrong in several ways, and Sims commented that the episode showcases "classic hostage tropes" including "the panicked cops, the slick negotiator [and] the snipers looking for a shot through their scopes".<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="DoG Mellor">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review-a-moralising-thriller/|title=Black Mirror season 5: Smithereens review – a moralising thriller|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Mellor|first=Louisa|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234605/https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review-a-moralising-thriller/|url-status=live}}</ref> Stephanie Dube Dwilson, writing for ''[[Heavy (website)|Heavy]]'', noted an absence of an "unexpected" or "incredibly dark" twist, as many prior episodes employ.<ref name="Heavy">{{cite web|url=https://heavy.com/entertainment/2019/06/black-mirror-smithereens-review/|title='Black Mirror' Smithereens Review: A Different Feel & a Strong Message|work=[[Heavy (website)|Heavy]]|last=Dwilson|first=Stephanie Dube|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234605/https://heavy.com/entertainment/2019/06/black-mirror-smithereens-review/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The episode suggests that social media companies are unaccountable and make people vulnerable and powerless.<ref name="Guardian"/><ref name="DoG Longo"/><ref name="BBC"/> Chris Longo suggested in ''Den of Geek'' that the technology is "purposely designed to give us tiny hits of dopamine".<ref name="DoG Longo">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-review-smithereens/|title=Black Mirror Season 5 Episode 2 Review: Smithereens|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Longo|first=Chris|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234608/https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-review-smithereens/|url-status=live}}</ref> The former [[Facebook]] president [[Sean Parker]] spoke in a 2017 event about the addictiveness of social media, saying that he, Facebook CEO [[Mark Zuckerberg]] and [[Instagram]]'s [[Kevin Systrom]] "understood this consciously" but "did it anyway".<ref name="Dazed"/> Mellor said that it is "gently ironic" that Chris uses a meditation app on his phone "to escape the effects of other apps".<ref name="DoG Mellor"/> The social psychologist Rosanna Guadagno highlighted that "research has shown that notifications from our phones have a negative impact on our stress levels, anxiety levels, and overall wellbeing".<ref name="S&F">{{cite web|url=http://www.scienceandfilm.org/articles/3246/people-as-commodity-black-mirrors-smithereens|title=People as Commodity: ''Black Mirror''{{'}}s "Smithereens|last=Guadagno|first=Rosanna|work=Sloan Science & Film|publisher=[[Museum of the Moving Image]]|date=28 August 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234620/http://www.scienceandfilm.org/articles/3246/people-as-commodity-black-mirrors-smithereens|url-status=live}}</ref> The song "[[Can't Take My Eyes Off You]]" occurs throughout the episode and plays in the closing credits; Mellor called the song choice "a gag about phone addiction".<ref name="DoG Mellor"/>

The episode shows social media companies as more powerful than law enforcement in profiling people.<ref name="Heavy"/> Guadagno saw Smithereen's information gathering on Chris as "both a violation of privacy" and a demonstration of "what you can learn about someone based on surveilling their digital activities".<ref name="S&F"/> Victoria Turk of ''Wired'' saw it unrealistic that Smithereen choose to get involved with police activity, saying that such companies "seem to constantly distance themselves" from this "as they don't want that responsibility".<ref name="Wired">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-smithereens-review|title=Review: 'Smithereens' is the least 'Black Mirror' episode ever|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|last1=Turk|first1=Victoria|last2=Reynolds|first2=Matt|date=7 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234611/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-smithereens-review|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Smithereens - Smithereen.png|thumb|alt=Smithereen|Critics identified the fictional Smithereen with the social media website [[Twitter]].]]

Critics most commonly compared Billy Bauer to Jack Dorsey, the CEO of Twitter at the time.<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="Vox"/><ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="BBC"/> Thomas Gorton of ''[[Dazed]]'' and ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]''{{'}}s Jim Vorel made comparisons to Zuckerberg, and Vorel also saw an aspect of [[Apple Inc.]] founder [[Steve Jobs]] in Billy.<ref name="Dazed"/><ref name="Paste">{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-review/|title=Andrew Scott Shines in Black Mirror's Otherwise Uneven "Smithereens"|work=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]|last=Vorel|first=Jim|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234611/https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-season-5-episode-2-review/|url-status=live}}</ref> Smithereen was identified as similar to Twitter, and Persona to Facebook.<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="Paste"/><ref name="Telegraph"/> Ed Cumming of ''[[The Independent]]'' commented of the name choice: "A smithereen is a tiny fragment of something, the debris of an explosion: the firm's users and also the information they post".<ref name="indy">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review-andrew-scott-netflix-charlie-brooker-a8943576.html|title=Black Mirror season 5: 'Smithereens' review – A thin premise that doesn't justify the running time|work=[[The Independent]]|last=Cumming|first=Ed|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605092624/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-5-smithereens-review-andrew-scott-netflix-charlie-brooker-a8943576.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Chris Longridge, writing for ''[[Digital Spy]]'', saw a "religious parable" in Billy, who could represent Jesus or a Christian God. Longridge described Billy as "effectively omniscient", with a "[[Renaissance art|Renaissance-art]] Jesus vibe". However, he "turns out to be just a guy", which could symbolise an "existential crisis of humankind in a world that no longer has God".<ref name="DS">{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/ustv/a27809123/black-mirror-smithereens-explained-god-jesus-religion/|title=Why 'Smithereens' is Black Mirror's first religious parable|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Longridge|first=Chris|date=7 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234612/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/ustv/a27809123/black-mirror-smithereens-explained-god-jesus-religion/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Reviewers gave differing descriptions of Chris's motives and behaviour. Olly Richards of ''[[NME]]'' said that Chris "holds Smithereen responsible" for his ex-fiancée's death, an easier choice "than accepting that he was at fault"; however, Longo said that when Chris talks to Billy, the audience learns that he "doesn't scapegoat Smithereen".<ref name="DoG Longo"/><ref name="NME">{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/blogs/tv-blogs/black-mirror-smithereens-review-contemporary-tragedy-corporate-responsibility-sexy-priest-2505308|title='Black Mirror': 'Smithereens' review – a contemporary tragedy about corporate responsibility (with Sexy Priest in it)|work=[[NME]]|last=Richards|first=Olly|date=6 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234612/https://www.nme.com/blogs/tv-blogs/black-mirror-smithereens-review-contemporary-tragedy-corporate-responsibility-sexy-priest-2505308|url-status=live}}</ref> Vorel said that Chris may be "at war with himself" over his choices, leading to "a spastic, explosive sort of nervous energy".<ref name="Paste"/> Sims saw the episode as "a tale of two totally adrift people"—Chris and Billy—"unable to continue living in an interconnected world".<ref name="Atlantic"/> Dwilson saw their conversation as exhibiting "the power of a simple one-on-one exchange in a world dominated by terse social exchanges".<ref name="Heavy"/> Guadagno hoped that after their call, Billy could "make his social media platform about maximizing positive human connection by making people the customer, not the commodity".<ref name="S&F"/>

[[Easter egg (media)|Easter egg]] references to previous episodes are made through frames of a character scrolling through contacts in their phone, many of whom share names with previous ''Black Mirror'' characters, and trending topics on Smithereen include SaitoGemu, a video game company from "[[Playtest (Black Mirror)|Playtest]]", and Tucker, the company behind simulated reality in "[[San Junipero]]".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27701098/black-mirror-smithereens-easter-eggs/|title=How 'Smithereens' connects to the Black Mirror expanded universe|last=Opie|first=David|website=[[Digital Spy]]|date=6 May 2019|access-date=7 June 2019|archive-date=7 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607144721/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27701098/black-mirror-smithereens-easter-eggs/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Critical response===
The episode received mixed reception, with most critics finding the storyline and subject matter lacking in complexity, but Scott's performance accomplished. On the review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the episode holds an approval rating of 65% based on 26 reviews. The website's critical consensus reads, "A slippery moral dilemma and a superb turn from Andrew Scott make 'Smithereens' watchable, even if its familiar story feels more like an early episode of ''Black Mirror'' than a fresh futuristic horror story."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s05/e02|title=Smithereens – Black Mirror Season 5|work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115170036/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s05/e02|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=6 February 2021}}</ref> Out of five stars, the episode garnered four stars in ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'', three in the [[BBC]] and ''The Independent'' and two in ''Vulture''.<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="BBC"/><ref name="Telegraph"/><ref name="indy"/> It received a rating of 7.8 out of 10 in the magazine ''Paste''.<ref name="Paste"/> ''[[Complex (website)|Complex]]''{{'}}s Frazier Tharpe thought the episode was the best of series five, but ''[[The Guardian]]''{{'}}s Lucy Mangan found it "perhaps least successful".<ref name="Guardian">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/05/black-mirror-season-five-review-charlie-brooker-miley-cyrus|title=Black Mirror season five review – sweet, sadistic and hugely impressive|work=[[The Guardian]]|last=Mangan|first=Lucy|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234611/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/05/black-mirror-season-five-review-charlie-brooker-miley-cyrus|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Complex">{{cite web|url=https://www.complex.com/pop-culture/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-netflix-review|title='Black Mirror' Season 5 Goes Back to the Basics For Its Best Netflix Season Yet|work=[[Complex (website)|Complex]]|last=Tharpe|first=Frazier|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605173636/https://www.complex.com/pop-culture/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-netflix-review|url-status=live}}</ref> Sims said it was the "only definite flop" of the series as it "suffers from many of the flaws" of the fourth one.<ref name="Atlantic"/>

Critics identified self-parody, drama and cliché as aspects of the episode, and mostly reviewed its tone negatively. Mellor said that it "feels like an imitation" of the "uniquely identifiable personality" of ''Black Mirror''.<ref name="DoG Mellor"/> Romano and Richards criticised the episode as reliant on clichés.<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="NME"/> Cumming summarised it as "muted rather than subtle" and Hugh Montgomery reviewed it for the BBC as "a rather inert and under-characterised drama".<ref name="BBC">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20190603-black-mirror-series-5-review|title=Black Mirror series 5 review|publisher=[[BBC]]|last=Montgomery|first=Hugh|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234614/https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20190603-black-mirror-series-5-review|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="indy"/> Longridge suggested that the episode may be "winking at the audience", given that it relates to a well-known parody of the show's message: "what if phones, but too much".<ref name="DS"/> Similarly, Mellor and Tharpe highlighted potential self-parody in Chris's rant upon discovering Jaden is an intern, though Tharpe found this nevertheless "emotionally affecting".<ref name="DoG Mellor"/><ref name="Complex"/> Tharpe also praised the episode as tense and "well-paced" yet "casually hilarious".<ref name="Complex"/>

The storyline and central theme were mostly criticised. As the longest episode of the series, "Smithereens" was criticised for length by Cumming and Sims, who both described the plot as "thin", as did Turk.<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="indy"/> Mellor said that it "lacks this show's usual depth", Turk found "the scope a bit narrow" and Richards viewed it as having "little to say that isn't already common opinion".<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="DoG Mellor"/><ref name="NME"/> Sims wrote that it was "hampered by{{nbsp}}... how long it takes for the action to get going".<ref name="Atlantic"/> The exploration of social media was reviewed by Turk to be "a bit two-dimensional" and Longo saw the episode as "too self-contained to fully realize the potential of the ideas".<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="DoG Longo"/> Montgomery wrote that the characters are "being held ransom to a plotline which is a vehicle for some rather clunky point-making" and Romano saw the message as "both redundant and a little weak".<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="BBC"/> Bramesco critiqued the episode as having a "strong concept with lots of avenues for deeper exploration" which was averted in favour of "the same old conclusion about smartphones exacerbating our worst qualities", while both Longo and Turk saw concerns about data privacy to be unsatisfactorily explored.<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="Wired"/><ref name="DoG Longo"/>

Some critics were disappointed by a lack of twists in the episode, while Chris's recounting of the car crash and the ending received mixed reception. Mangan and Reynolds both said that the episode did not "twist and turn" as much as it should have and Sims "kept waiting for a twist that never really arrived".<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="Guardian"/> Reynolds found the storyline predictable from the 15 minute mark onwards, though Dwilson was "never quite sure where the episode was heading" and mostly guessed incorrectly.<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="Heavy"/> Longo saw Chris's "big reveal" about the cause of the car crash to be "devastating", but Romano said it "simply doesn't land with much impact".<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="DoG Longo"/> Mellor saw the ending as a "more subtle and effective point about social media", but Richards said it "falls flat" and Bramesco called it a "contrived non-ending".<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="DoG Mellor"/><ref name="NME"/>

[[File:Andrew Scott TV BAFTAs 2019.png|thumb|alt=Andrew Scott|[[Andrew Scott (actor)|Andrew Scott]]'s acting received praise even among some negative reviews.]]
Andrew Scott's role as Chris received critical acclaim. Several critics found that his performance was the highlight of an otherwise poor episode, such as Sims, who said that Scott's "committed lead performance" made him "at least interested throughout", and Reynolds, who said that Scott "just about held [the episode] all together".<ref name="Wired"/><ref name="Atlantic"/> Benji Wilson of ''The Telegraph'' found that his "astonishing control and range{{nbsp}}... elevated a too-tidy plot".<ref name="Telegraph">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-smithereens-review-andrew-scott-astonishing-grief/|title=Black Mirror: Smithereens, review: Andrew Scott is astonishing as a grief-stricken taxi driver gone rogue|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Wilson|first=Benji|date=5 June 2019|access-date=7 February 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605072908/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-smithereens-review-andrew-scott-astonishing-grief/|url-status=live}}</ref> Montgomery called the character "a compellingly twitchy, ambiguous presence", while Mangan said Scott had "uniquely potent and peculiar energy" which is "perfectly channelled" into Chris.<ref name="Guardian"/> Longo said that the acting is "unnerving throughout", but that Scott "dials it up to a 10" in the phone call with Billy.<ref name="DoG Longo"/> Bramesco viewed it differently, saying that Scott "feels like he's starting at a ten and leaving himself nowhere to go" and finding Scott unconvincing in the phone call, "seemingly uncertain whether the moment should be played hysterically or for genuine pathos".<ref name="Vulture"/> While Cumming found Chris to be "the only developed character", Longo said that the episode "missed key chances to add depth" to Chris.<ref name="DoG Longo"/><ref name="indy"/>

Other actors and characters received more mixed reception. Montgomery found Grace "an amusing Jack Dorsey parody", and Dwilson "appreciated how his character surprised [her]" in his relatability.<ref name="Heavy"/><ref name="BBC"/> Vorel, in contrast, found it "rather difficult" to empathise with Billy.<ref name="Paste"/> Idris received praise for his role from Dwilson and Romano.<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="Heavy"/> The storyline involving Hayley was criticised as "undercooked" by Cumming and "extraneous frippery" by Bramesco, but Vorel found the nature of her attempting to log into her daughter's Persona account every day a "powerful, [[Sisyphean]] piece of imagery".<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="Paste"/><ref name="indy"/>

Hawes received praise from Romano as he "keeps the pace taut", while Longo analysed that he "deliberately shot Chris' reactions to the use of phones in a cafe to cast a shadow of isolation around him" and used "flashback", "foreshadowing" and "purposeful misdirection".<ref name="Vox"/><ref name="DoG Longo"/> ''Pitchfork'' rated the soundtrack 6.8 out of 10, for being effective but lacking "iconic melodies". The reviewer, Martin-McCormick, found that the track "Meditation App" would fit in "the lobby of a high-end spa", but did not recommend the other tracks as standalone music.<ref name="Pitchfork"/>

===Episode rankings===
"Smithereens" ranked poorly on critics' lists of the 23 instalments of ''Black Mirror'', from best to worst:
{{col-begin}}
{{col-2}}
* 11th – [[James Hibberd (writer)|James Hibberd]], ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/gallery/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/?slide=6443800#6443800|title=Every Black Mirror episode ranked|date=9 April 2020|author=[[James Hibberd (writer)|Hibberd, James]]|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115155856/https://ew.com/gallery/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/?slide=6443800|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
* 11th – Ed Power, ''The Telegraph''<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-best-episodes-worst-ranked/|title=Black Mirror: best and worst episodes ranked, from Striking Vipers to San Junipero|date=5 June 2020|first=Ed|last=Power|website=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115155347/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-best-episodes-worst-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
* 15th – Matt Miller, ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|title=Every Episode of Black Mirror, Ranked|date=5 June 2019|first1=Corey|last1=Atad|first2=Matt|last2=Miller|website=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115155037/https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>

{{col-2}}
* 19th – Morgan Jeffery and Rosie Fletcher, ''Digital Spy''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|title=Ranking all 23 episodes of Charlie Brooker's chilling Black Mirror|date=13 June 2019|first1=Morgan|last1=Jeffery|first2=Rosie|last2=Fletcher|work=[[Digital Spy]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111225039/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|archive-date=11 November 2020|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
* 20th – Aubrey Page, ''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked From Worst to Best|date=10 October 2020|first=Aubrey|last=Page|work=[[Collider (website)|Collider]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115154650/https://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
* 21st – Tim Molloy, ''[[TheWrap]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thewrap.com/striking-vipers-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-san-junipero-ashley-san-junipero/|title='Striking Vipers' to 'San Junipero': Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Good to Mind-Blowing (Photos)|date=8 June 2019|first=Tim|last=Molloy|website=[[TheWrap]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201113105133/https://www.thewrap.com/striking-vipers-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-san-junipero-ashley-san-junipero/|archive-date=13 November 2020|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
* 21st – Charles Bramesco, ''Vulture''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html|title=Every Black Mirror Episode, Ranked|date=5 June 2019|first=Charles|last=Bramesco|website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115160525/https://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>
{{col-end}}

''[[IndieWire]]'' authors ranked the 22 ''Black Mirror'' instalments excluding ''Bandersnatch'' by quality, giving "Smithereens" a position of 11th.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Worst to Best|last1=Greene|first1=Steve|last2=Nguyen|first2=Hanh|last3=Miller|first3=Liz Shannon|work=[[IndieWire]]|date=24 November 2017|access-date=15 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203010214/https://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|archive-date=3 December 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Instead of by quality, Proma Khosla of ''[[Mashable]]'' ranked the episodes by tone, concluding that "Smithereens" was the 10th-most pessimistic episode of the show.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' episode ever, ranked by overall dread|date=5 January 2018|first=Proma|last=Khosla|work=[[Mashable]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115161226/https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref>

===Awards===
{{See also|List of awards and nominations received by Black Mirror}}
As the fifth series of ''Black Mirror'' consisted of three episodes that do not tell a complete story, it was not initially clear whether it would compete in TV Movie or Limited Series or Drama Series categories of the [[Emmy Awards]]. After Netflix petitioned to allow "Smithereens" as a TV Movie, despite a new rule that entries must be 75 minutes or longer, it was initially reported that it would be nominated in this category. Later, the [[Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]] announced that the episode would instead be competing as a Drama Series, where performers who appear in less than 50% of a series have the choice to compete in leading, supporting, or guest awards.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/race/emmys-black-mirror-episode-not-waived-tv-movie-category-1294621|title=Emmys: 'Black Mirror' Episode Not Waived in to TV Movie Category (Exclusive)|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|last=Feinberg|first=Scott|date=14 May 2020|access-date=25 January 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234615/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/race/emmys-black-mirror-episode-not-waived-tv-movie-category-1294621|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2020/05/black-mirror-booted-emmys-tv-movie-category-1202231500/|title=Is 'Black Mirror' Emmy Dominance Over? Series Booted From 2020 TV Movie Race|work=[[IndieWire]]|last=Sharf|first=Zack|date=15 May 2020|access-date=25 January 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234615/https://www.indiewire.com/2020/05/black-mirror-booted-emmys-tv-movie-category-1202231500/|url-status=live}}</ref> Scott was nominated for the [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series|Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series]] category. The winner was [[Ron Cephas Jones]] for ''[[This Is Us]]''.<ref name="Emmy">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2020/09/2020-emmy-winners-list-1234585914/|title=Emmys 2020: All of This Year's Winners and Nominees|date=20 September 2020|first=Steve|last=Greene|work=[[IndieWire]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210113143900/https://www.indiewire.com/2020/09/2020-emmy-winners-list-1234585914/|archive-date=13 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=13 January 2021}}</ref>
